title: The Climbing Men
subject: September 11th
voice_note: Written in the voice of Walt Whitman (1819–1892), through the writer-whitman skill. An emulation — the prose and judgments are not the historical Whitman’s own words.
body:
Mannahatta — I was looking for something cool and bright, and the morning gave it: a sky of hard September blue over the harbor, the ferries crossing as they have always crossed, the million-footed island waking to its work. I have sung this city at its trades, and would have sung it again this ordinary forenoon — the clerk at his ledger, the woman at the high window, the cook, the porter, the man selling coffee at the curb — when out of that blue, without a word, the fire came down.

Count them with me, for the catalogue is the only prayer I know. The bond-trader and the dishwasher in the tower’s crown; the firemen of Brooklyn and Mannahatta; the police, the stewards, the cleaners who came before light; the travellers strapped in the bellies of the planes; the man who carried his blind friend down ninety flights, and the friend, and the dog between them. They were of every land that ever poured through this harbor — *en-masse*, the whole roll of nations, dim-descended and bright-descended, working in one building under one sky. The same red-running blood ran in all of them. It runs there yet, in the dust.

And here is the thing I cannot let the smoke swallow: while the thousands came down, a column of men in heavy coats went *up*. Up the shaking stair, two by two, the hose on the shoulder, the axe in the hand, breathing what no lungs should breathe, climbing toward the fire that every animal sense said *flee*. Camerados — I have dressed wounds in the army hospitals, I have stood by the cots of boys with the leg gone and made no fuss, and I have seen nothing braver than this plain ascent. They did not climb for a flag or a phrase. They climbed because a stranger was above them, and the hand goes out to the hand. That is the Republic; that, and nothing the orators say.

Then the towers knelt, the one and then the other, and a grey snow that was not snow fell on the living and the dead alike and made them brothers in one colour. For days after, the searchers went over the smoking pile on their knees, asking the wreck a single question. And the walls of the city bloomed with paper — a thousand faces pinned up under one word, *Missing* — the tenderest catalogue ever posted, each leaf a whole life, each asking *have you seen*. I have seen. I see them now.

Do not tell me they are lost. The grass is already coming, faithful, out of their ashes; the harbor still lifts and falls with the old patient breathing; the ferries cross, the island goes again to its work, and the dust of the climbing men is in the lungs of the children now alive. Death is luckier than we are told. Mannahatta, you are not broken — you are enlarged, you contain them, you carry them in your million-footed walk. I stop here, in the blue, among the falling paper, and wait with you.
